The internal water-control process requires identifying the physical water path, distinguishing backup from surface water, flood, seepage, plumbing discharge, and roof entry, and referring recurring, unclear, poorly maintained, or unresolved drainage and plumbing conditions.

The New York guide gives a 60-day-after-discovery internal diary and communication target for a suspected water-backup claim, while the attached HO 01 31 contract separately governs prompt notice, mitigation, preservation, acknowledgment, decision, and payment timing.

The internal New York guide requires referral for 3 paid property claims within the preceding 3 years and prohibits binding the referred risk until the underwriting decision is documented; this is an internal threshold rather than a legal rule, policy limit, or automatic coverage result.

Prior-loss review must consider cause, location, severity, disposition, repair status, recurrence, current condition, and source consistency; unresolved, disputed, open, unclear, or repair-unverified losses require internal referral and a documented referral package.

Internal renewal review covers changed eligibility, exposure, valuation, occupancy, condition, loss potential, repairs, inspections, ownership, and current claims; adverse action must be classified accurately, based on verified information, and supported by recorded underwriting direction before customer-facing processing.

Under the current DFS-2016-02 position represented in the repository, New York notice periods are 60 days before expiration for nonrenewal, 20 days before the effective date for cancellation other than nonpayment, and 15 days before the effective date for cancellation for nonpayment; notices must identify the action and provide specific, accurate reasons.

DFS-2016-02 requires claims-based cancellation or nonrenewal to use relevant and accurate verified claims information, distinguish claims from inquiries, correct erroneous or misattributed records, state a specific claims reason, and take corrective action when disputed information undermines the notice.

For the historical DFS-2010-09 position, the repository source states 45 days before expiration for nonrenewal and 20 days before cancellation for reasons other than nonpayment, and the cited historical notice provision does not state a numeric nonpayment-cancellation period.

The internal New York claims procedure requires prompt file creation or update, recording of loss facts and evidence, reasonable mitigation within 7 days after discovery as an internal control, investigation before a coverage position, neutral fraud referral, and documented closure.

The HO 01 31 contract requires prompt claim notice and cooperation, allows inspection and evidence requests, requires preservation of damaged property when reasonably possible, and states 15-day acknowledgment, 15-business-day acceptance or rejection after requested information, and 5-business-day payment of an accepted claim.

DFS-2018-11 places responsibility for the New York homeowners data call on the admitted insurer despite delegated service-provider activity, requires legal-entity identification and insured-risk location reporting, and requires reconciliation, authorized certification, correction, and supporting-record retention.

New York Rule 530 adds internal referral controls for vacancy, short-term lodging, business and business indicators, specified recreational and animal exposures, unrepaired or unsafe property conditions, structural or renovation concerns, nonstandard ownership or occupancy, and material conflicts among addresses or carrier records; referral holds the affected action for direction and is not itself a declination or coverage result.

Although the New York appetite guide allows incidental home activity when it does not change the residential character, Manual Rule 530 requires any business activity at the premises to be evaluated before binding; this is an internal referral control rather than a New York legal requirement.

Manual Rule 900 sends a New York risk with roof age at or beyond 25 years to declination processing and prohibits binding without an authorized exception; the age control is separate from the appetite guide’s condition evidence and from contract settlement treatment.

Manual Rule 900 refers requested water-backup coverage above $25,000 to underwriting authority and prohibits quoting that requested limit as available while review is pending; this internal limit control does not create coverage or replace cause-and-condition analysis.

New York internal loss controls have distinct source-owned thresholds: the appetite guide refers 3 paid property claims in the preceding 3 years, Rule 530.B refers any risk with 3 paid property claims without stating that lookback, Rule 700.D refers a renewal risk with 2 paid property claims during the current policy term, and Rule 900.C requires three years of loss history and referral when incomplete.

Manual Rule 700 requires every renewal file to be reviewed for changes affecting eligibility, exposure, valuation, occupancy, or loss potential; it treats inspection reports as valid for 12 months and requires referral for specified occupancy, property-condition, system, or water concerns.

Manual Rule 800 contains internal task timings of 10 days for a premium-default notice and 45 days for a notice of intent not to renew, but those numbers are not the controlling New York external notice periods and must not shorten the applicable DFS or contract requirement.

Manual Rule 310 requires internal referral and a hold on binding authority for a reported loss at or above $100,000, prohibits binding, renewal, or broader coverage while a claim is open, and suspends underwriting action for disputed claims; Rule 900.A separately routes a reported loss exceeding $25,000 to claims authority and prohibits settlement outside delegated authority.

North Carolina homeowners underwriting uses a three-layer boundary: the appetite guide and Rule 550 are internal eligibility, referral, evidence, and authority controls; NCDOI-2018-03 and NCDOI-2021-06 govern disclosure and claims administration; and HO 01 32 controls only the contract provisions it changes when attached.

The NC internal appetite permits Coverage A from $150,000 through $1,000,000, requires a roof inspection before binding at roof age 18 years or greater, requires a wind-mitigation inspection when Coverage A exceeds $500,000, and refers two paid property claims in the preceding three-year review.

NC delegated authority permits binding Coverage A up to $700,000 only when the risk otherwise fits the approved appetite; requests above that amount must be referred before terms are offered, and the exposure must not be split or restructured to evade referral.

NC roof underwriting requires current, supportable evidence of age, material, condition, repairs, and serviceability, and requires referral or hold for leakage, deterioration, structural distress, defective details, unresolved storm damage, obscured condition, or unsupported future repair; an internal roof rule is not a claim-settlement exclusion.

NC water-risk review begins with the physical source and path and requires referral or hold for active or recurring water conditions, unresolved moisture, drainage or below-grade entry, defective plumbing or protective devices, and incomplete remediation; water-backup eligibility and limits must be taken from the actual endorsement and declarations rather than from an internal referral rule.

For an attached HO 01 32, the contractual windstorm-and-hail deductible applies only to covered loss directly caused by windstorm or hail and is between 1% and 5%; an increase requires written notice at least 30 days before its effective date, and a Named Storm Period or Seacoast Territory does not itself create coverage.

The NC loss-history control reviews the preceding three years and refers two paid property claims, but also requires evaluation of cause, recurrence, repair quality, mitigation, current condition, discrepancies, and unresolved hazards rather than relying on claim count alone.

The internal NC claims handoff opens and documents the claim promptly, verifies the policy package, protects property, uses a seven-day-after-discovery mitigation checkpoint and a 60-day suspected-water-backup intake target when practicable, investigates cause and scope, requests relevant evidence, escalates complex or adverse matters, and closes only after known issues are resolved.

For the applicable NC contract and claims bulletin, claim receipt is acknowledged within 30 days, a claim is accepted or rejected within 30 business days after needed requested items are received, and an accepted claim is paid within 30 business days after payment becomes due; written decisions must identify relevant policy provisions and material facts.

NCDOI-2018-03 requires a clear, conspicuous, understandable, retainable fungi, wet-rot, dry-rot, or bacteria limitation disclosure, including the statement that the most the insurer will pay is $5,000, for applicable policy transactions; the disclosure must match the policy and cannot create or alter coverage.

When HO 01 32 is attached, its contract states a $5,000 maximum for all loss caused by fungi, wet or dry rot, or bacteria and requires express coverage for such loss; a fungi allegation or observation still requires reasonable investigation and a written, policy-based explanation before limitation or denial.

NCDOI-2021-06 keeps the insurer responsible for claims handled by employees, adjusters, producers, administrators, vendors, and other representatives and requires procedures, supervision, training, quality review, privacy controls, complaint escalation, and records sufficient to show the basis for material decisions.

A required NC referral remains on hold until authorized direction is recorded and conditions are satisfied; approval is risk- and term-specific, verbal assurance or silence is not approval, material changes require reassessment, and the underwriting file must retain the trigger, sources, authority, conditions, communications, and final disposition.

The NC underwriting record must distinguish reported from verified facts, record sources and dates, preserve discrepancies and adverse information even when a risk is accepted, document authority and referral reasons, and retain completion evidence before closing a corrective requirement.

North Carolina underwriting records must tie each material decision to the operative transaction package and preserve state-specific evidence: verify the North Carolina HO-3 policy/form position, effective date, and attached HO 01 32 (2018-05) when applicable; retain the matching fungi disclosure with delivery and filing or approval records; and preserve dated claim-handoff records and delegated-party oversight when a loss is routed.

The Underwriting Referral and Authority Matrix is internal underwriting and claims guidance rather than an insurance contract, and it cannot create, expand, restrict, or waive coverage; applicable policy terms control coverage and payment.

A referral is a request for direction rather than an automatic approval, declination, coverage grant, or transfer of file responsibility; silence, delay, informal discussion, or an incomplete response does not constitute approval.

Line underwriting may bind Coverage A up to and including $800,000, senior underwriting may bind up to and including $1,500,000, and requests above the applicable authority must be referred before binding.

Coverage A authority is applied to the amount actually requested at binding and cannot be bypassed by informally reducing the limit, splitting related transactions, relying on another account's approval, or changing approved terms without renewed authorization; endorsements affecting Coverage A remain part of the authority review.

The Matrix requires referral when material risk facts cannot be reconciled, unusual occupancy, condition, protection, or loss characteristics affect the decision, or available information does not support a confident authority determination.

The Matrix requires referral at or above 25 years of roof age and when roof age, replacement status, condition, material, or required condition assessment cannot be reliably established, including active leakage, deterioration, unrepaired storm damage, conflicting evidence, or unusual construction.

For wind and hail underwriting, a wind mitigation inspection is required when Coverage A exceeds $1,000,000, and referral is required for conflicting or incomplete mitigation evidence, deteriorated or damaged roofs or openings, recurring or unresolved storm losses, or requests to alter the applicable deductible.

The Matrix requires referral for a requested water backup limit above $25,000, prohibits binding that referred request until documented approval, requires source differentiation from surface water, flood, seepage, and maintenance conditions, and requires referral for out-of-authority term changes.

A risk with two paid property claims must be referred, available loss history covering three years must be reviewed, and a referred risk must not be bound until underwriting review and authority are documented; incomplete, recurring, unexplained, misrepresented, or repair-unverified losses also require escalation.

State appetite rules can impose earlier or stricter risk controls without enlarging delegated authority: Texas requires a roof inspection at or above 15 years and does not permit binding at or above 25 years, while the Matrix separately requires referral at or above 25 years and line authority remains capped at $800,000.

The 2024-03 HO-3 form excludes sewer, drain, and sump backup unless a water-backup endorsement is attached, while the Matrix supplies the operational source-confirmation and greater-than-$25,000 referral rules rather than changing that contract treatment.

The 2024-03 HO-3 form applies the dwelling's applicable loss-settlement basis to roof surfacing, including replacement-cost treatment when its 80% insured-to-value condition is met, unless an actual cash value roof schedule endorsement is attached; HO 23 74 2025-05 requires ACV for roof surfacing when Roof Age is 12 years or greater and permits age to be established from reliable records or observations. Matrix H.0.15 and H.2.19–H.2.24 keep these contract settlement rules separate from underwriting eligibility and require operational review or referral when the age, condition, or related settlement issue is material or cannot be reliably assessed.

A usable referral package identifies the requested decision, requested Coverage A limit and material facts, relevant policy and loss information, conflicts and verification efforts, and the approval response, approver, conditions, and material communications retained in the underwriting record.

While a referral is pending, staff may continue fact gathering unless a hold applies but must not represent coverage as approved or bound; after direction is received, the action must match the expressly approved terms and conditions.

For claims and other handling matters, the Matrix requires a handling file, factual intake without premature coverage characterization, referral of matters outside assigned authority, complete information to the reviewer, required authority before payment or settlement, and final documentation before closure.

Underwriting review must keep four decisions separate: appetite eligibility determines whether the presented risk fits the applicable state/product profile, delegated authority determines whether the handler may bind the exact exposure and terms, referral rules determine when action must pause and how it is dispositioned, and the issued policy package determines contract coverage; an approval in one layer does not substitute for another.

The general delegated Coverage A ceilings are $800,000 for line underwriting and $1,500,000 for senior underwriting, with referral required above the applicable role limit; Texas is stricter because its appetite range ends at $1,200,000 and Manual Rule 510 routes amounts above $800,000 through $1,200,000 to senior review and amounts above $1,200,000 to decline or referral.

Manual Rule 300 is the delegated-binding control: it requires sufficient and material risk information, active delegation, recorded requested limit and authority, documented approval before binding referred risks, and binding only within approved terms.

Manual Rule 310 creates mandatory referral and hold outcomes for listed triggers such as a reported loss at or above $100,000, open or disputed claims, liability allegations, litigation, material application inconsistencies, suspected misrepresentation, and unverifiable ownership; Manual Rule 320 separately requires decline when a known materially loss-increasing condition cannot be corrected before binding.

Manual Rule 900 is a separate appendix routing matrix: it sends reported losses exceeding $25,000 to claims authority, new business above $1,500,000 to senior underwriting, incomplete three-year loss history to referral, roof age at or beyond 25 years to declination processing, and water-backup coverage above $25,000 to underwriting authority; these positions must not be merged with Rule 310 or the Referral Matrix thresholds.

For Texas homeowners transactions, Manual Rule 510 requires verification of the Texas risk address before quoting or binding, confirmation of insurable interest, matching occupancy to actual use, and referral of conflicting ownership or occupancy information; these are state operating controls and do not change policy coverage or enlarge delegated authority.

This page is internal Texas underwriting guidance: it governs risk selection, referrals, authority, and file handling, but it does not change policy coverage, contractual duties, or Texas law; the assembled policy, declarations, forms, endorsements, and applicable law control those matters.
The Texas homeowners appetite accepts Coverage A from $150,000 through $1,200,000 and requires a protection class of 8 or lower, subject to the separate delegated-authority limits.

Texas roof underwriting requires verification of roof type, condition, age, and repair evidence; roofs at least 15 years old require inspection before binding, roofs at least 25 years old are not bindable, and unknown age or material condition concerns require referral or additional evidence.

The Texas guideline treats leakage, moisture intrusion, material roof deterioration, exposed substrate, sagging, drainage failure, temporary or incomplete repairs, ponding, uncertain specialty materials, damaged transitions, and improperly secured roof equipment as roof-condition referral triggers rather than routine binds.

For Coverage A over $500,000, the Texas guideline requires a qualified wind-mitigation inspection retained in the file and referral of conflicts among the inspection, application, photographs, or other underwriting evidence; prior wind, hail, roof, and water losses require explanation and repair evidence.

Wind and hail deductible handling is edition-specific: HO 01 45 (2022-01) uses a 1%-10% deductible range with at least 45 days' notice for an increase, while DP 01 45 (2022-01) uses a 1%-5% range with at least 30 days' notice; each form's Named Storm Period continues 72 hours after the governmental or official designation ends.

Texas Bulletin B-2021-08 operationally constrains windstorm-and-hail deductible administration by addressing minimum and maximum deductible categories, disclosure, calculation basis, consistency, duplicative deductibles, increase notice, and named-storm-period disclosure; it does not replace the applicable policy deductible term.

The internal water-backup appetite allows only controllable sewer, drain, or sump exposures, requires review of prior entry, drainage and sump conditions, lower-level exposure, protective devices, and maintenance, and refers unresolved plumbing or repeated-overflow conditions and requested limits above $25,000.

The cited HO 04 90 (2027-01) endorsement constrains water-backup implementation with a $10,000 contractual limit, a $1,000 deductible, a backwater-valve requirement for finished areas below grade, and a 30-day notice condition; these form terms must not be replaced by the internal $25,000 referral threshold or the guideline's 60-day handling checkpoint.

Texas prior-loss review covers the preceding 3 years and requires referral when there are 2 paid property claims, counting dwelling, other-structure, personal-property, and loss-of-use claims including claims paid by another insurer; unresolved required referrals block binding until resolved and documented.

The Texas guideline requires an internal mitigation checkpoint within 7 days after discovery of a covered loss condition, prompt evidence preservation and cause evaluation, documentation supporting adverse or payment decisions, and escalation of fraud, disputes, unusual coverage issues, and potential bad-faith allegations; applicable policy and endorsement deadlines still govern contractual handling.

Delegated Texas authority permits a line underwriter to bind up to $800,000 Coverage A and a senior underwriter up to $1,200,000; requests above $1,200,000 must be declined or referred, and reviewers may not split or restructure an exposure to evade the ceiling.

Referral is required for unusual or unresolved construction, condition, occupancy, maintenance, valuation, inspection, loss, or other material facts, exceptions to stated requirements, changed facts, missing or conflicting verification, and actions outside authority; approval, evidence, conditions, inspections, and waivers must be retained before binding or declining.

Texas internal attachment controls require a requested endorsement to be supported by current risk facts, eligible, and matched to the named insured, location, and insured property; water-related endorsements additionally require evaluation of water and drainage conditions and referral of repeated drainage or sewer concerns, while the attached form remains the source of contractual terms.

Before offering, attaching, or excepting a Texas windstorm or hail deductible arrangement, internal Rule 400 requires current-fact, eligibility, and matching review and Rule 510 requires the deductible to be available and supported, with exceptions referred; the issued HO or DP form and Texas bulletin separately govern contract and regulatory administration.

The Personal Lines Underwriting Manual and referral matrix are internal operational guidance rather than policy terms or coverage grants; binding and coverage decisions must remain separate from the applicable policy form, declarations, endorsements, and other controlling requirements. A referral is a request for authorized direction, not approval, declination, or a transfer of responsibility for the file.

Rule 300 sets two Coverage A delegated ceilings: a line underwriter may bind through $800,000 and a senior underwriter may bind through $1,500,000; requests above the applicable ceiling must be referred and the requested amount and authority used must be recorded.

Rule 300 requires the risk to be within active delegation and requires a documented approval before a referred risk is bound; pending, verbal, changed, inactive, backdated, split, or transaction-sequenced handling cannot substitute for authorized terms.

Before binding, Rule 300 requires verification of effective date, identity, insurable interest, occupancy, location, territory, material hazards and loss information, claim activity, property condition, valuation, coverage fit, deductible, and material rating information; unresolved material conflicts are referral conditions.

Rule 310 makes a reported loss at or above $100,000 a mandatory underwriting referral with binding held pending disposition, and separately requires referral for open or disputed claims, bodily-injury or property-damage allegations, negligent supervision, intentional conduct, pending litigation, and demands indicating a potential claim.

Rule 310 requires referral for adverse prior underwriting actions, hazard-related declines by another carrier, inconsistent application information, suspected material misrepresentation, unverifiable ownership, and trust, estate, or similar ownership arrangements.

Rule 310 requires referral for business, commercial storage, manufacturing, repair, processing, public access, vacancy or unoccupancy, renovation, unrepaired structural or foundation conditions, roof or water concerns, plumbing and sanitation issues, mold, fungi, and rot.

Rule 310 requires referral for electrical, heating, fuel, solid-fuel, pool, recreational, animal, firearm, vehicle, operator, rental, lodging, shared-occupancy, organized-event, fraud, identity, credit, investigation, inspection, protective-feature, unusual-construction, and other material-hazard conditions identified in the rule.
Rule 320 is the Manual's no-clearance path: a known condition that materially increases expected loss and cannot be corrected before binding is declined, and underwriting notes cannot cure it.

Rule 320 requires decline for unresolved structural, foundation, roof, water-intrusion, plumbing, electrical, heating, fire, moisture, building-envelope, premises-safety, water-feature, recreational, animal, and bodily-injury hazards described in the rule.

Rule 320 requires decline for abandoned or hazardous property, ongoing construction or major alteration, vacancy or neglect, unlawful or disputed occupancy or ownership, unrepaired or recurring losses, misrepresentation, refused access, unverifiable information, criminal activity, contamination, earth movement, unresolved drainage or weather damage, and restricted emergency access.

Rule 320 requires decline for impaired protection, unresolved protection gaps, replacement-cost or coinsurance concerns, commercial or unacceptable occupancy uses, material neglect, unsupported professional repairs, and disputed material conditions; an unlisted condition that cannot be cleared before binding is referred under Rule 320.54.

Rule 900 separately directs claims-authority referral for a reported loss exceeding $25,000 and underwriting referral for new business Coverage A above $1,500,000, while Rule 310 uses an at-or-above $100,000 underwriting-loss trigger; these are separate source positions and functions rather than one universal threshold.

Rule 900 requires three years of loss history and referral of incomplete history, while the referral matrix and Texas appetite guide separately identify two paid property claims in the preceding three years as a referral trigger; the Manual appendix does not state that claim-count threshold.

Rule 900 refers roof age at or beyond 25 years for declination processing and requires a recorded authorized exception before binding, while the Texas appetite guide separately requires inspection at 15 years and says a roof at or above 25 years may not be bound; these are recorded as separate source positions.

Rule 900 requires referral for water-backup coverage above $25,000 and bars treating the requested limit as available pending review; the referral matrix uses the same underwriting trigger, while the HO-3 base form separately excludes sewer, drain, and sump backup unless an endorsement is attached.

Rule 900 provides a compact appendix checklist for application and inspection discrepancies, unrepaired damage, occupancy and use, valuation and maintenance, structural and liability hazards, prior insurance and loss information, property-system and protection concerns, unusual construction or access, exceptions, post-bind changes, and unclear eligibility; the appendix requires evidence and a recorded disposition.

The referral control flow is: collect and verify material facts, test appetite and active authority, hold and document a referral when the test fails or is unclear, continue permitted fact gathering while approval is absent, then compare approved terms and conditions with the requested action before binding; material changes require renewed direction.
The Personal Lines Underwriting Manual is internal carrier direction for personal-lines acceptance, referral, and file handling and is not intended for external use.
The Manual constrains underwriting action but does not grant or alter policy coverage; coverage is determined by carrier-issued coverage terms.
Underwriters must act within delegated authority, apply Manual direction before binding, refer risks outside authority or requiring referral, and may not split a risk to avoid an authority limit.

Before completing an underwriting decision, the underwriter must use current reliable information, verify material risk characteristics, resolve or refer missing and conflicting material information, and document the decision and referral basis.
Manual authority decisions must be approved through authorized channels, approval conditions must be applied exactly, and required conditions may not be waived without authorized approval.
The corpus distinguishes frozen form and bulletin authority from living manuals and guidelines, so internal underwriting guidance does not replace the issued form text.
HO-3 eligibility requires Coverage A of at least $150,000, refers limits above $1,500,000 and protection classes above 8, and accepts only owner-occupied dwellings used as the insured's residence.

HO-3 rules require sound property condition and refer material roof, structural, exterior, storm, fire, water, electrical, heating, plumbing, drainage, moisture, and renovation concerns; the named insured must have an insurable interest and risks failing eligibility are declined.

HO-5 eligibility requires Coverage A between $300,000 and $2,500,000, protection class 6 or better, and an owner-occupied dwelling; rental, transient, vacant, construction, major renovation, and unrepaired-damage risks are referred.

HO-5 rules refer unsafe or uncertain roofs, repeated water intrusion, structural movement, unsafe systems, unusual heating or fuel, business or agricultural use, material liability hazards, adverse loss history, open claims, unreliable valuation, and incomplete or conflicting underwriting information; failing comprehensive eligibility results in decline or authority referral.

HO-4 provides no Coverage A dwelling insurance while Coverage C covers eligible personal property, and Rule 130 requires a tenant-occupied private residence, insurable interest in contents, protection class 9 or better, and a complete identifiable address.

HO-4 rules decline vacancy and refer uncertain primary-residence occupancy, rooming or boarding, subletting, undisclosed shared occupancy, material business or care activity, unusual contents, construction, unrepaired damage, unsafe systems, catastrophe or security concerns, and incomplete or conflicting information.

HO-6 eligibility permits Coverage A only from $5,000 through $250,000 and requires a legally established condominium unit with an insurable interest that is used as a private residence by the named insured; non-condominium interests, transient use, and unsuitable active construction are referred or declined.

HO-6 underwriting must verify the condominium association's master coverage and the unit owner's repair responsibility, use a default dwelling limit only when reliable evidence does not support another selection, and refer materially limited association coverage, building-level hazards, disputed responsibilities, and unusual or commercial property exposures.

DP-3 eligibility requires lawful residential occupancy, an applicant insurable interest, sound and serviceable construction, Coverage A of at least $75,000, referral approval before binding above $750,000, and a supportable replacement-cost estimate.

DP-3 rules refer deferred maintenance, roof, foundation, electrical, heating, plumbing, drainage, unresolved water or fire damage, vacancy or inadequate care, seasonal unattended occupancy, construction, impaired protection, access problems, wildfire or coastal exposure, flood or earth movement concerns, and related site hazards; the Manual directs vandalism handling after 30 consecutive days of vacancy.

DP-3 rules refer business, agricultural, transient, boarder or roomer use, hazardous detached-structure storage, code or historic concerns, nontraditional construction, land-only or incomplete properties, uncertain ownership or control, and unresolved application, inspection, valuation, or loss discrepancies; risks outside eligibility or authority must be referred before disposition.

The HO-3, HO-5, HO-6, and DP-3 forms describe different covered property and dwelling exposures, so the product-line Manual rules must be applied without rewriting the respective form grants, exclusions, limits, or settlement terms.

Rules 400 and 410 are internal underwriting controls: they govern whether an endorsement or deductible option may be selected and issued, but they do not grant coverage, change a policy deductible, or replace the applicable policy forms and endorsements.

Rule 400 requires review of every requested endorsement before binding or renewal, attachment only for an eligible risk supported by current and complete information, matching to the named insured, location, and insured property, and referral or suspension when eligibility or material facts are uncertain.

Rule 400 requires underwriting review of water and drainage, plumbing, roof, electrical, heating, use, occupancy, construction, prior losses, safeguards, and pending claims when those facts affect an endorsement, with referral for unresolved or adverse conditions.

Rule 400 prohibits using an endorsement to cure an ineligible risk, requires appropriate wording and no duplicate coverage, and requires effective-date alignment rather than retroactive attachment for a known loss circumstance.

Rule 400 requires approved processing, post-processing confirmation, renewal reassessment, and a clear record of the facts, rationale, and authority for every endorsement attachment, revision, or removal; unaddressed endorsement issues must be referred before issuance.

The authority matrix requires referral of a requested water-backup limit above $25,000 and prohibits binding the referred request until documented approval; this is an internal authority threshold, not a contractual water-backup limit.

Rule 410 sets the Section I all-other-perils deductible selection floor at $500, requires the selected option to be supported by risk characteristics, and requires the selection to be documented; this is an internal underwriting floor rather than a universal policy deductible.

Rule 410 requires use of an available deductible for the applicable coverage part, prohibits inferring an unstated deductible or combining terms from separate proposals, and requires referral of conflicting, unavailable, unsuitable, or exceptional deductible requests.

Rules 410.M and 410.N require application of the available named-storm minimum and wind-deductible ceiling but do not state numeric values; the applicable contract and state overlay supply the actual parameter, and requests outside normal authority require referral.

Rule 410 requires deductible selections to be consistent with submission, rating, issuance, location, occupancy, construction, protection, property use, and cause-of-loss information, and prohibits using a deductible to offset unacceptable property conditions or satisfy premium preference.

Rule 410 requires current-information review for deductible changes, prohibits retroactive application and post-loss revision based only on claim information, requires capture of the final selection before binding, and requires completion of deductible review before issuance.

HO 04 90 (2027-01) is effective only when attached, preserves unmodified policy terms, and contractually applies a $1,000 deductible to covered water-backup damage from the same occurrence; Rules 400 and 410 constrain attachment and internal selection without changing that contractual deductible.

HO 23 74 (2025-05) leaves the applicable policy deductible in force and applies it after the endorsement's roof-surfacing adjustment; Rules 400 and 410 constrain roof-related attachment and selection but do not replace the contractual deductible or settlement sequence.

HO 23 77 (2022-07) contractually applies a 2% to 10% windstorm-or-hail percentage deductible based on the applicable limit, while Rule 410.N constrains internal selection to the applicable underwriting ceiling and Rule 400 constrains weather-related attachment without changing the endorsement's stated percentage.

The endorsement-training workflow requires reading the complete endorsement rather than relying on its title, comparing its operative changes and deductible treatment with the request and existing endorsement set, and checking the complete package against the correct insured, policy term, location, property, effective date, schedules, and referenced pages. A listed-but-missing endorsement, an unlisted attachment, a blank or unclear schedule, or a mismatch between system text and issued wording must be clarified or reconciled before issuance.

For deductible-related attachments, the review must identify the loss cause and property to which the deductible applies, distinguish special deductible treatment from the general deductible, and confirm current risk facts, eligibility, selected wording, schedule details, and effective application before issuance; the issued wording must be preserved and corrected through the approved process rather than informal edits.

The HO-3 2024-03 base form makes the Section I deductible a contractual term with a minimum of $1,000, applies it to covered loss unless modified by endorsement, and requires application according to the policy terms and applicable endorsement; this contractual floor is distinct from Manual Rule 410.A's internal $500 selection floor.

When attached, HO 04 90 2027-01 provides its stated water-backup and sump-discharge-or-overflow coverage subject to a $10,000 section limit and supplies a $1,000 deductible applied to covered water-backup damage arising from the same occurrence; the endorsement's attachment language preserves unmodified policy terms and does not create a separate contract.

HO 23 74 (2025-05) changes settlement for covered roof surfacing without changing the applicable policy deductible; for composition shingle subject to its age-based treatment, the form uses a 20% payable percentage when Roof Age is at least twelve years, and the roof-surfacing adjustment is applied before the deductible.

HO 23 77 (2022-07) supplies an edition-specific contractual windstorm-or-hail percentage deductible range of 2% to 10%, calculated from the applicable limit and applied before payment; when a state amendatory form is also attached, its Declarations-based deductible terms must be checked separately rather than assuming the HO 23 77 range controls every policy. Texas HO 01 45, for example, requires its Declarations windstorm-and-hail deductible to be 1% to 10% and applies it separately from another deductible.

Rules 600 and 610 are internal underwriting controls: Rule 100 prohibits using the Manual to alter coverage, and Rule 600 makes inspection evidence part of risk selection and file handling rather than stating a premium, deductible, settlement, or coverage result.

Rule 600 requires an inspection when underwriting information is incomplete, inconsistent, or unreliable and prohibits binding until the issue is resolved or an authorized exception is recorded; it also requires the trigger, information needing verification, and binding disposition to be documented.

Rule 600 requires a roof survey before binding when roof age reaches 15 years, with evidence addressing roof condition, materials, installation quality, and visible deterioration, and requires the reported age, request, findings, and underwriting action to be recorded.

Rule 600 supplies inspection or referral triggers across property condition, occupancy and security, structural and moisture concerns, systems and site conditions, premises hazards, business or construction use, prior damage, discrepancies, utilities, code notices, access limitations, conflicting external data, unresolved recommendations, and unusable photographs.

Inspection evidence must come from a reliable source with sufficient authority and relevant expertise; altered, incomplete, or unverifiable material cannot be relied on, and the file must identify the source, verification performed, evidence reviewed, and action taken.

Rule 610 requires underwriting to record receipt and verification dates, source attribution and limitations, and material discrepancies, and to resolve a conflict before completing action when it affects eligibility, classification, or terms.

Rule 610.AA says an inspection report is valid for “18 from its completion” but does not specify a unit; the completion date and use decision must be recorded, and unclear Manual direction must be escalated rather than converted into an invented validity period.

Rule 600 requires prompt review of inspection findings, referral of hazards outside normal authority, and no waiver of material conditions without authorized approval; Rule 610 requires the file to state the operational decision, basis, follow-up, eligibility findings, and authority used.

Corrective requirements must address a material inspection condition, state an objective required outcome, and identify due status and verification method; completion must be supported by reliable evidence rather than an unsupported verbal statement, with remaining concerns and closure action recorded.

The inspection process may close only after every material finding is resolved, referred, or accepted within authority, with final inspection status, outstanding conditions, authority applied, and final underwriting action preserved; withheld access, requested evidence, or material information must be documented and any adverse action must follow applicable procedures.

Rule 610 requires an audit-ready underwriting record that preserves material facts and sources, terminology, timing, discrepancies, decisions, referrals, conditions, eligibility findings, risk characteristics, inspection findings, authority, restrictions, adverse-action rationale, corrections, and quality-review resolution.

Rule 610 requires professional and factual notes, prompt recording of material actions, preserved correction history, and documented approval for departures from underwriting direction; Rule 600 requires inspection reports, photographs, communications, and related evidence to be protected in the underwriting file with access limited to legitimate underwriting purposes.

Rule 600 and 610 underwriting controls are separate from HO-3 2024-03 post-loss duties: the form requires an insured to protect property and keep repair records, preserve and show damaged property, permit inspection, provide requested records and claim evidence, and submit to examination when reasonably requested; it separately requires requested inventories and ownership or lien information, while stating that an inspection is not acceptance of a condition or representation and is not a warranty that property is safe, sound, or compliant with law.

State appetite overlays are separate from Rule 600: California requires an acceptable roof inspection before binding at 20 years or greater, review of available roof photographs, documented completion of active-leak repairs, and controlled handling of incomplete roof work, plus a wind-mitigation inspection above $1,000,000 Coverage A; Texas requires a roof inspection before binding at or above 15 years, prohibits binding at or above 25 years, and requires a wind-mitigation inspection above $500,000 Coverage A.

Rules 230–250 are internal underwriting controls for risk selection, referral, evidence, and acceptance; they must be applied before binding within delegated authority and do not alter the coverage grant in the issued policy.

A pending referral is not approval: the underwriter must hold the affected binding, renewal, change, or endorsement action, use an authorized recorded channel, and satisfy approval conditions exactly before acting.

Rule 230 requires referral for material premises-liability hazards including unsafe pools and water features, recreational and elevated structures, animals, weapons or explosives, business or visitor activity, rental or lodging, hazardous property conditions, and unresolved premises disputes.
Rule 230 requires a swimming-pool barrier at least 4 feet high and requires correction or acceptable control of damaged barriers and gates that do not close and latch securely before acceptance.

Rule 230 does not state a separate dollar authority level or numeric clearance period; its watercraft provision refers to an applicable outboard-horsepower threshold without stating the horsepower number, so the current controlling source must be obtained rather than inferred.

Rule 240 requires prior-loss review before accepting, renewing, or changing a risk, covering the preceding 3 years and including reported, paid, denied, and open property claims where available; applicant disclosures must be compared with approved loss sources.

Rule 240 requires referral of a risk with 2 paid property claims in the applicable history and prohibits binding without underwriting authority; its large-loss referral provision names a threshold but does not state the amount.

Rule 240 evaluates loss cause, recurrence, current condition, and repair quality rather than claim count alone, and requires referral when remediation or cause correction is unclear, including repeated water loss, unresolved roof or electrical concerns, and prior premises-liability hazards.

Rule 240 permits reliable repair evidence such as photographs, invoices, contractor statements, and inspection reports, but requires referral for incomplete, altered, or inconsistent evidence and does not permit binding while a required prior-loss referral remains unresolved.

Rule 250 requires verification of occupancy before binding or continuing, distinguishes resident use from seasonal, intermittent, nonprincipal, temporary, and unoccupied use, and requires prompt notice of a material change from owner to nonowner occupancy.

Rule 250 directs application of the vacancy condition when customary occupants and personal property are absent and states that vandalism is excluded after 60 days of vacancy; it does not provide a numeric deadline for its prompt-notice requirement.

The Manual's Rule 250 60-day vacancy position is distinct from DP-3 Rule 150.N, which separately states 30 consecutive days for vandalism handling; these internal product positions must not be presented as a new contract exclusion.

Rule 250 requires referral and verification for tenant, rental, short-term rental, home-sharing, lodging, mixed occupancy, detached-structure occupancy, subleasing, unauthorized occupants, and unclear possession or maintenance arrangements; rental review includes lawful access and landlord-contents ownership.

Rule 250 requires a final supported occupancy, vacancy, and rental classification before underwriting action and prohibits binding or continuing when reasonable inquiry leaves material occupancy facts unresolved.

Manual Rule 300 supplies general delegated authority ceilings of Coverage A through $800,000 for a line underwriter and through $1,500,000 for a senior underwriter, while the Texas appetite separately states a $150,000–$1,200,000 eligible Coverage A range; these are separate eligibility and authority constraints rather than coverage limits.

HO 04 42, HO 24 71, HO 24 73, and HO 24 82 provide distinct contractual liability or personal-injury grants only according to their attached terms; an underwriting referral does not change those terms and an attached endorsement does not automatically clear an internal eligibility or hazard referral.

HO 24 71 sets a $100,000 maximum for covered business-pursuit damages and applies it to the total damages regardless of the number of insureds, claimants, claims, or suits; HO 04 42 provides its stated liability coverage only for a lawful incidental occupancy conducted at premises used in connection with the residence, subordinate to residential use, and not materially changing the residential character.

Rules 200, 210, and 220 are internal pre-bind and renewal underwriting controls for property risk selection, referral, holds, conditions, and documentation; they do not alter coverage, which remains governed by the applicable carrier-issued form, declarations, and attached endorsements.

Rule 200 requires construction information to be complete and classified by predominant exterior-wall construction, requires reliable protection-class verification, and refers unsupported construction, access, fire-water, and response information before final underwriting action.

Rule 200 requires a wind mitigation inspection before final underwriting action when Coverage A exceeds $750,000 and requires review of material roof, attachment, and opening-protection information when wind exposure is material.

Rule 210 requires roof inspection findings before binding at roof age 15 years or greater and holds binding authority until acceptable condition is supported; it requires decline at roof age 25 years or greater without discretionary override.

Rule 210 requires reliable evidence for roof age and replacement scope and refers deteriorated, damaged, leaking, inadequately repaired, materially worn, inaccessible, or otherwise unverified roof conditions; required corrections must be completed and documented before binding when necessary.

Rule 220 requires identification of water sources and prior water damage and requires referral of active leakage, moisture staining, mold evidence, wet materials, or unresolved water entry; binding may not proceed while the Rule 220.C condition remains unresolved.

Rule 220 routes plumbing, appliance, water-heater, freeze, vacancy, drainage, sump, sewer, septic, check-valve, and recurring-water-loss conditions to evidence review, corrective action, or referral when the source or repair status is unresolved.

Rule 220 requires referral for a requested water-backup limit above $25,000 and requires the backup deductible to be available for and approved by underwriting, with authorized approval before alteration; when attached, the water-backup endorsement controls the contractual limit and deductible. HO 04 90 (2027-01) states a $10,000 limit of liability and a $1,000 deductible for each covered water-backup loss.

Rule 210's roof-age thresholds constrain underwriting eligibility rather than claim settlement; when attached and applicable, HO 23 74 2025-05 separately applies actual-cash-value treatment to covered roof surfacing at Roof Age 12 years or greater using reliable age evidence.

When Rule 220 water-exposure information is insufficient, the Manual prohibits binding until the missing information is obtained or authorized direction is recorded and requires a clear note of the condition, evidence, referral activity, and final action.

Rule 100 makes inspection currency and referral records part of the general underwriting lifecycle by treating an inspection report as current for 12 months after receipt, requiring resolution of material inspection concerns before final action, and requiring authorized approval conditions to be recorded.

Rules 310 and 320 overlay the detailed property controls: Rule 310 mandates referral with a binding or processing hold for open or disputed claims, vacancy or unoccupancy, ongoing renovation, structural or roof damage, recurring water intrusion, unresolved plumbing leakage, sewer or drain backup, and suspected mold, fungi, or rot; Rule 320 requires decline when a known materially loss-increasing condition cannot be corrected before binding, including unresolved roof damage or leakage, active water intrusion, unrepaired plumbing failure, and unresolved active mold, fungal growth, rot, or moisture damage.

Rule 240.S requires review of prior claims involving mold, fungi, bacteria, rot, or moisture and referral when the moisture source is unresolved or remediation is incomplete; the fungi-and-bacteria aggregate does not determine underwriting eligibility.

HO 04 90 (2027-01) separately excludes loss caused by mold, fungus, wet rot, dry rot, bacteria, virus, or other microorganisms even when the condition results from water backup or sump discharge, and addresses odor, staining, contamination, testing, monitoring, assessment, and remediation only as its wording allows.

Personal Lines Underwriting Manual Rule 700 requires every renewal file to be reviewed for changes affecting eligibility, exposure, valuation, occupancy, or loss potential, and requires material changes, unresolved underwriting conditions, and conflicting or unavailable information to be resolved or referred before renewal terms are released.

Rule 700 requires referral of a renewal risk with two paid property claims and directs review of loss cause, severity, recurrence, corrective action, open claims, and known circumstances that may lead to a claim; the claim-count threshold is an internal underwriting referral control rather than a policy limit.

Rule 700 treats an inspection report as valid for 12 months and requires updated information when it is no longer valid or conditions may have changed; conflicting inspection information must be reconciled before renewal terms are finalized.

Rule 700 identifies incomplete repairs, roof or exterior deterioration, water intrusion or repeated water damage, unsafe systems, vacancy or unoccupancy, changed occupancy or use, business or short-term rental activity, ownership changes, and material construction, valuation, protection, or hazard changes as renewal review or referral concerns.

Rule 700 requires a renewal outside assigned authority or relying on a continuing exception to have recorded current approval, and Rule 800 requires the referral or adverse-action file to preserve the basis, verified facts, authority response, approver, conditions, and final disposition.

Rule 800 requires the proposed transaction to be classified as cancellation, nonrenewal, withdrawal, or binding suspension, then requires policy-status verification, a supportable basis, verified information, jurisdiction review, approved reason language, correct policy and insured identification, approved delivery, and a hold when required facts or approval are missing.

Rule 800 contains internal instructions for a 10-day premium-default notice and a 45-day notice of intent not to renew, but those internal timing controls do not replace controlling state law, regulator requirements, or policy-form notice periods.

For the current New York position represented by DFS-2016-02 and HO 01 31 2016-04, nonrenewal requires at least 60 days before expiration, cancellation for a reason other than nonpayment requires at least 20 days, and nonpayment cancellation requires at least 15 days; notices require specific action, policy, effective-date, and reason information, and claims-based action requires relevant and verified claims information.

For Florida HO 01 09 2023-07, the contract form states 10 days for nonpayment cancellation, 45 days for another permitted cancellation, and 135 days for nonrenewal; separately, OIR-2023-04 requires at least 120 days and specific roof-related content for a roof-age or roof-condition nonrenewal, so the applicable policy edition, action type, and regulatory requirement must be checked rather than merged into one number.

Renewal and adverse-action files must retain the material facts and sources, loss and repair evidence, inspection review, referral and approval record, action classification, policy status, applicable jurisdiction and policy edition, timing analysis, notice version and content, delivery evidence, corrections, and final policy status.

Rules 500–570 are internal carrier underwriting controls for state-specific eligibility, authority, referrals, exceptions, and file documentation; they are not policy terms, coverage grants, or regulator bulletins.

A pending state-exception referral does not authorize binding: the underwriter must record the trigger, evidence, requested action, response, authority, conditions, and final disposition before completing the affected action.

Florida Rule 500 requires a roof inspection at age 15 or older, declines roofs at age 20 or older, sets Coverage A from $200,000 through $900,000, and limits line and senior authority to $600,000 and $900,000 respectively.

Florida Rule 500 refers repeated water, fire, liability, occupancy, business, animal, recreational, ground-movement, weather-loss, ownership, claims, maintenance, access, and inspection concerns, and requires state-exception support and complete file documentation for decisions.

Texas Rule 510 permits line authority through $800,000 Coverage A, sends amounts above that and through $1,200,000 to senior underwriting, declines or refers amounts above $1,200,000, refers water-backup limits above $25,000, and requires a roof inspection at age 15 or older.

Texas Rule 510 requires address, insurable-interest, occupancy, property, roof, loss, protective-device, system, deductible, and exception verification; it requires complete approval support before binding or declining and timely review for the applicable accept-or-deny deadline.

California Rule 520 sets a $1,000,000 line-underwriter ceiling, prohibits Coverage A above $2,000,000, requires 100% insured-to-value support for internal replacement-cost eligibility, and requires authorized direction for quake-deductible changes.

California Rule 520 refers unrepaired roof or fire damage, wildfire and vegetation hazards, open claims, nontraditional occupancy, construction, site instability, unsafe systems, protection gaps, material discrepancies, and unsupported mitigation; it requires a complete file for referrals, exceptions, and adverse decisions.
New York Rule 530 binds Coverage A through $750,000, requires referral for three paid property claims, and allows state-exception credits only when eligibility and support are confirmed.

New York Rule 530 refers unresolved damage, vacancy, lodging, business or agricultural use, unsafe premises and systems, recreational and animal hazards, occupancy and ownership conflicts, and requires underwriting direction before an intent-not-to-renew notice.

Louisiana Rule 540 declines roofs at age 20 or older, limits line authority to $500,000 Coverage A, sets a $750,000 Coverage A ceiling, and refers missing, conflicting, deteriorated, or incompletely repaired roof conditions.

Louisiana Rule 540 refers water, occupancy, business, recreational, animal, loss, claims, inspection, systems, drainage, flood, and backwater-valve concerns; it also refers unavailable maximum windstorm-and-hail deductible options, submissions outside the internal named-storm window, and unsupported exceptions while requiring final decision support.

North Carolina Rule 550 refers Coverage A above $700,000, requires a roof inspection at age 18 or older, refers changes to the fungi-and-bacteria aggregate, and refers requests exceeding the seacoast deductible ceiling.

North Carolina Rule 550 refers unresolved ownership, occupancy, construction, structural, loss, protection, access, coastal, water, hazard-material, valuation, and information issues, and requires authority-backed documentation for exception actions.

Colorado Rule 560 requires a roof inspection at age 12 or older, declines roofs at age 22 or older, requires review of the roof-schedule trigger age, refers Coverage A above $850,000 to appropriate authority, and refers wind deductibles above approved handling.

Colorado Rule 560 refers wildfire, vegetation, access, fire protection, heating and freeze, water, occupancy, business, animal, recreational, solar and energy-storage, structural, weather, construction, ownership, inspection, evidence, and protective-device concerns, and requires a complete file for referred or declined risks.

Illinois Rule 570 refers Coverage A above $700,000, water-backup limits above $15,000, and sewer-backup limits inconsistent with the described premises; it declines material application information that cannot be verified.

Illinois Rule 570 refers water, roof, systems, loss, occupancy, business, security, inspection, protected-class, consumer-reporting, exception, valuation, hazardous-storage, claim, and litigation concerns, prohibits protected-class underwriting, requires recorded exception approval, and requires a complete file.
Rules 500, 510, 520, 540, and 550 direct underwriters to use the rating manual’s state-exception pages as support for credits and to remove or refer unsupported or disputed credit treatment.

The rating workflow requires a complete submission before final rating, records the source of each material input, holds incomplete submissions, and performs a final reasonableness review; material changes or unresolved conflicts must be documented and can require re-rating or referral.

Material rating inputs include occupancy, location and territory, construction, dwelling age, roof information, use, form selection, replacement-cost valuation, dwelling limit, deductibles, catastrophe exposure, prior losses, open claims, and protective devices; the rating file must preserve the supporting facts and decisions.

The Personal Lines Underwriting Manual is internal acceptance and referral direction within delegated authority; it requires current reliable information and recorded decisions, and it must not be used to alter or interpret contractual coverage.

Form selection must match property type, occupancy, and requested coverage rather than a preferred premium, and the rating record must identify the selected form; the representative source forms distinguish HO-3, HO-5, HO-6, and DP-3 product lines and editions.

Replacement-cost valuation must use approved methodology, be compared with the dwelling limit, and support the selected coinsurance and extended-replacement-cost treatment; material variances or uncertain valuation require documentation and referral.

The rating manual sets an internal AOP deductible floor of $500, requires an available system option matched to the coverage package and location, prohibits unauthorized custom deductibles, and requires premium recalculation when the deductible changes.

Peril-specific, named-storm, and wind deductible treatment must remain distinct from the AOP deductible and must be supported by approved system and underwriting parameters; unsupported or over-limit requests are referrals.

The representative current form texts do not share one universal contractual deductible minimum: HO-3 and HO-5 state $1,000, HO-6 states $500, and DP-3 states $1,500, so the rated deductible must be reconciled to the applicable form, Declarations, endorsements, and state wording.

The generic protective-device rating rule grants a 15% central-station discount only after risk-specific evidence verifies the device serves the insured location and rated structure, is installed and operational, remains active, and is not removed, bypassed, disconnected, or impaired.

Protective-device evidence must identify the monitoring arrangement, provider, address, communication path, and hazard-specific function; generic product material, brand names, or one protective function cannot establish another, and overlapping credits cannot be stacked unless rating logic permits it.

The generic roof rule permits a 20% new-roof credit only for completed, location-specific replacement supported by evidence; proposals, localized patching, cosmetic work, incomplete work, or work on an outbuilding do not establish eligibility.

Roof condition is evaluated as a system, with material deterioration, leakage, damaged covering, structural irregularity, unrepaired storm damage, impaired drainage, or failed components potentially requiring surcharge or referral; a surcharge is removed only after evidence supports correction of its cause.

The generic windstorm rule permits a 35% opening-protection credit only for complete, current, location-specific protection covering the relevant rated openings and structure; installed, serviceable, accessible, compatible protection must be verified rather than inferred from ordinary glazing, decorative shutters, stored materials, or vague renovation statements.

Wind mitigation eligibility and wind percentage deductible treatment are independent reviews; a mitigation credit does not change the deductible, and prior credit cannot automatically continue after an opening is altered or replaced.

Endorsement premium selection uses the approved premium table only after matching the eligible endorsement, option, risk characteristics, rating basis, and flat or per-limit premium basis; a limit-based factor is applied to the premium developed before that adjustment and the selection is documented.

Part 12 state exceptions can replace generic adjustment values and add state-specific checks: the cited exception material includes 45% opening protection, 10% new-roof, and 10% central-station values, and separately requires a 15% earth-movement deductible when earthquake coverage applies; these values must not be universalized.

The final rating file must allow reconstruction of the submission, selected classification and form, valuation and deductibles, every adjustment and endorsement charge, supporting evidence, referral or approval, and final system output; unsupported or conflicting inputs require hold, removal of the adjustment, authorized resolution, or re-rating.
